summary: Defines an XML format for watcher information, the dynamic state describing who has subscribed to a resource and in what condition. It is the data format used with the SIP watcher information event package.

eli5.summary: This is the form a presence service fills in to list the people watching your status, written in a standard layout.

questions: what is a watcher in sip
what is the watcherinfo version attribute
subtitle: An XML document layout for listing who is subscribed to a resource and what state each subscription is in.

tldr.problem: Watchers subscribe to information about a resource, and the combined state of those subscriptions changes as subscribers come and go. Someone who wants to follow that state needs an agreed data format for it.
tldr.mechanism: A watcherinfo XML document holds watcher-list elements, one per resource, each containing watcher elements with an id, a status and an event. Documents carry a version number and are marked either full or partial.
tldr.outcome: A watcherinfo subscriber can merge a stream of full and partial documents into one table per resource. The format is used for subscriber authorization in SIP-based presence.

today: RFC 3858 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the data format that goes with the watcher information event package in RFC 3857.

sections.title: Watchers and Watcher Information
sections.content:
A watcher is an entity that subscribes to information about a resource, using the SIP event framework from RFC 3265. Each subscription carries state, such as who the subscriber is and what condition the subscription is in. The union of that state for all subscriptions to one resource is the watcher information for the resource.

Because this state changes over time, it is useful to subscribe to it too. The RFC's main example is a user finding out who has subscribed to their presentity, so that the user can decide whether to authorize each subscription. Two pieces are needed for that: a SIP event template-package, specified in RFC 3857, and a data format, which is what this RFC defines.
sections.eli5: Imagine a list of everyone who asked to keep an eye on your lemonade stand. This RFC says how to write that list down so every computer reads it the same way.

sections.title: Structure of a Watcherinfo Document
sections.content:
A watcher information document is an XML document that MUST be well-formed and SHOULD be valid. It MUST be based on XML 1.0 and MUST be encoded in UTF-8. Its namespace is the URN urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:watcherinfo.

The root element is watcherinfo. It holds any number of watcher-list elements, one per watched resource. Both of its attributes MUST be present. version orders the documents: it starts at 0, goes up by one for each new document sent to a watcherinfo subscriber, is scoped within one subscription, must fit in a 32 bit integer and does not wrap. state says whether the document holds the full state or only the watchers that changed since the previous document (partial).

Each watcher-list has a mandatory resource attribute (a URI for the watched resource) and a mandatory package attribute (a token naming the event package). Elements and attributes from other namespaces MAY appear for extensibility, and unknown ones MUST be ignored.
sections.eli5: The document is a folder with a version sticker on the front. Inside are one sheet per thing being watched, and each sheet lists the watchers.

sections.title: The Watcher Element
sections.content:
The watcher element describes one watcher. Its value is a URI for the watcher, which SHOULD be the authenticated identity as determined by the server processing the subscription. That is usually an address-of-record such as sip:joe@example.com, not a device address.

Three attributes are mandatory. id is a unique identifier for the subscription, written as a token as defined in RFC 3261, and it MUST be unique across all watchers reported in a given watcherinfo subscription. status gives the state of the subscription and event gives the event that caused the move to that status. Their meanings come from RFC 3857.

Three optional, informative attributes exist: display-name, expiration (seconds from now until the subscription expires) and duration-subscribed (seconds from the SUBSCRIBE that created it to now). The xml:lang attribute MAY give the language of the display name.

What a subscriber sees depends on authorization. A user subscribing to watcher information for someone else's presence may be told only about themselves, while the owner sees all watchers, and an administrator could see all watchers for all resources.
sections.eli5: Each watcher entry is a name tag: who they are, a secret ID number for the sign-up, and whether you said yes. Extra notes like their nickname are optional.

sections.title: Computing Watcher Lists
sections.content:
A watcherinfo NOTIFY usually carries only the watchers whose state changed, so a subscriber has to combine notifications over time. It keeps one table per watcher list, identified by the resource URI, with one row per watcher, indexed by the id. Each table also has a version number, started from the version of the first document received.

For each new document the subscriber compares versions:

  • One higher than the local version: increase the local version and process the document.
  • More than one higher: set the local version to the new value, process the document, and SHOULD send a refresh request to trigger a full state notification.
  • Lower than the local version: discard the document without processing.

A full document means all tables are flushed and rebuilt from the document. A partial document updates the tables: a missing table is created, a missing row is added, and an existing row is overwritten with the new state. A row whose state becomes terminated MAY be removed at any time.
sections.eli5: Each note says what changed. You keep a notebook and number the notes. If you notice you missed one, you ask for a fresh full copy of the list.

sections.title: Example and Schema
sections.content:
The RFC's example describes a presentity who is a professor, with two watchers. The document is version="0" and state="full", and its one watcher-list covers sip:professor@example.net for the presence package. userA is active after the event approved, and userB is pending after the event subscribe.

The RFC also gives an XML Schema. It limits state to full or partial, and status to pending, active, waiting or terminated. The event attribute may be subscribe, approved, deactivated, probation, rejected, timeout, giveup or noresource.
sections.eli5: The example shows a professor with two people on the list: one the professor already said yes to, and one still waiting for an answer.

sections.title: Security and IANA Registrations
sections.content:
Watcher information is sensitive. The protocol used to distribute it SHOULD ensure privacy, message integrity and authentication, and should provide access controls that restrict who can see whose watcher information.

The IANA section registers the media type application/watcherinfo+xml, with no mandatory parameters and a file extension of .wif or .xml, and the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:watcherinfo. The registration says the document type has been used to support subscriber authorization functions for SIP-based presence.
sections.eli5: A list of who is watching you is private, so only the right people should be allowed to look at it.
